description: Macaca fascicularis, also known as the crab-eating macaque or cynomolgus macaque, is the most widespread non-human primate in Southeast Asia and the only old-world monkey known to use stone tools in daily foraging. Lives in matrilineal groups of 10-85 individuals with female philopatry (females stay, males emigrate at puberty). Omnivorous and frugivorous — despite the name 'crab-eating,' they primarily eat fruits but also crabs, insects, and small vertebrates. Known for robbing and bartering behavior at tourist locations. Has 10 recognized subspecies. The most traded primate species and most popular in scientific research. Listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List in 2022. One of the 100 most invasive species globally, though this status is debated. Unique among terrestrial mammals for violating the Wallace Line, found across the Lesser Sunda Islands.
population_estimate: No precise global total available. Extremely widespread with large populations in some areas but declining overall. On Mauritius, population estimated at 35,000-40,000 in mid-1980s-90s, dropped to as low as 8,000. Listed as Endangered (2022) due to population declines exceeding 50% over three generations, driven by trapping for trade. The most traded primate species globally.
habitat: Native range encompasses most of mainland Southeast Asia, Malay Peninsula, Singapore, Sumatra, Java, Borneo, Philippines, Nicobar Islands, and Lesser Sunda Islands. Rare terrestrial mammal found on both sides of the Wallace Line. Lives in wide variety of habitats: primary lowland rainforests, disturbed and secondary rainforests, shrubland, riverine and coastal forests, nipa palm and mangrove forests. Thrives near human settlements — synanthropic species. Prefers disturbed habitats and forest periphery. Introduced to Mauritius, West Papua, Ngeaur, Tinjil Island, Kabaena Island, and Kowloon Hills (Hong Kong).
threats: Overexploitation — the most traded primate species, heavily trapped for biomedical research
The most popular species used in scientific research globally
Habitat loss and fragmentation from deforestation
Human-wildlife conflict, perceived as agricultural pests
Considered invasive in some regions (Mauritius), leading to culling
ecosystem_role: Major seed disperser — spreads seeds of many fruit-bearing plants across forests. Pollination through flower visitation and movement. Prey for large predators like clouded leopards, pythons, and birds of prey. Plays complex ecological role: as a 'weed species' it thrives in disturbed habitats and secondary forests, contributing to forest regeneration. Debated impact on native birds in introduced ranges.
human_connection: Deeply intertwined with human culture: seen as smart, adaptive, sacred (at some Hindu temples), pests, or research subjects. Known generically as 'kera' in Indonesia and Malaysia. The most traded primate and most used in biomedical research globally — critical for pharmaceutical testing. Robbing and bartering behavior at tourist locations is a fascinating example of primate economics. In Mauritius, macaques are perceived as sacred, tourist attraction, pets, pests, and food — all at once.
what_students_can_do: Do not feed wild macaques — it creates dependence and dangerous human-wildlife conflict
Secure food and trash when visiting areas with wild macaques
Learn about the ethics of primate use in biomedical research
Support habitat conservation protecting native primate populations
Educate others not to keep macaques as pets (they are wild animals, not pets)
fun_fact: This is the ONLY old-world monkey known to use stone tools — they crack open shellfish and nuts just like early humans!
They have learned to barter with humans — in some tourist areas, they steal valuables and only return them for food!
Despite their name 'crab-eating,' they actually prefer fruit — crabs are just a small part of their varied diet
They are one of very few mammals found on both sides of the Wallace Line, a major biogeographical boundary in Indonesia
They share about 93% of their DNA with humans, which is why they are so widely used in medical research
